title: Open the Window
author: Christopher Perrin
summary: Christopher Perrin begins on a flight from Denver to Chicago, where nearly every window shade is closed while passengers watch screens inches from a view that would have astonished almost every human who ever lived. He recalls that the Wright brothers first flew only 123 years ago and notes how quickly the miraculous has become ordinary. His own habit is to take a window seat and remind himself that he is flying. The scene becomes an image for education: children arrive full of wonder, asking why the moon follows the car and why the sky is blue, and teachers and parents risk dimming that appetite. Perrin cites Aristotle's claim that philosophy begins in wonder, so that wonder awakens curiosity and invites patient, joyful learning. His closing appeal is simple: keep the windows open.
points: Perrin uses the closed airplane shades as a compact image of how familiarity and screens dull our attention to marvels that are right in front of us.
He treats wonder as the starting point of education rather than an optional ornament, grounding the claim in Aristotle.
Children's constant questions are presented as delightful evidence of a natural appetite for knowing that adults should nurture rather than be exhausted by.
The implied charge to teachers and parents is to recover their own sense of wonder so that learning begins in delight and not in compliance.
quotes: Nearly everyone was watching a movie or television show on a small screen, while just inches away, on the other side of the window, lay a view that would have astonished nearly every human being who ever lived.
Today we scarcely notice. We buckle our seat belts, sip coffee, watch a movie, and arrive a thousand miles away a couple of hours later.
Children are naturally full of wonder. They ask why the moon follows the family car, why birds can fly, why the stars shine, why the sky is blue.
A child enters the world with an appetite for knowing, a natural desire to understand the marvelous world into which he has been born.
Wonder is not an optional ornament of education. It is where education begins.
Aristotle understood this more than two thousand years ago when he observed that philosophy begins in wonder.
Wonder awakens curiosity, and curiosity invites us into the patient and joyful work of learning.
